section_summary: This section contains two transmitting despatches from the Acting Political Adviser in Tokyo and the beginnings or complete texts of two SCAP Civil Information and Education Section research reports. The first report surveys the demilitarization and democratic reconstruction of Japanese physical education during the first two years of the Occupation, including curricula, teacher training, health programs, equipment shortages, sports organizations, and conferences. The second report begins a history of foreign students in Japan from 1896 to 1947, emphasizing Chinese students, former colonial students, and Japan’s efforts to attract students from elsewhere in Asia.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 217: Postwar Developments in Japanese Physical Education
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of a SCAP special report on postwar developments in Japanese physical education.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser encloses a Civil Information and Education Section report dated March 15, 1948. The report concerns the reconstruction of physical education in Japan after the war.

subfiles.title: Special Report AR-305-E-C-4: Postwar Developments in Physical Education Through the First Two Years of the Occupation
subfiles.from: Education Research, Analysis and Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Examines the removal of militarism from Japanese physical education and the construction of a democratic postwar program.
subfiles.summary: The report traces physical education from the Meiji period through its increasing subordination to military drill, budō, wartime mobilization, and ultranationalist objectives. It then describes Occupation and Ministry of Education measures that eliminated military practices, screened teachers, introduced democratic curricula, and promoted games, sportsmanship, health, and local initiative. Detailed sections cover conferences, the 1947 Guide to Physical Education, decentralization, short training courses, equipment shortages, school lunches, health programs, and sports organizations. Appendices describe budō, the organization of the Bureau of Physical Education, and physical-education conferences held from 1945 through 1947, followed by sources and conference interviews.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 255: Transmittal of Report—Foreign Students in Japan, 1896-1947
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of a SCAP research report on foreign students in Japan between 1896 and 1947.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies the enclosed report as a compilation prepared by the Civil Information and Education Section. It outlines chapters on Chinese and colonial students, the International Students Institute, and wartime and postwar conditions, noting the numerical predominance of Chinese students and the relatively small Western contingent apart from about 3,000 foreign-born persons of Japanese ancestry.

subfiles.title: Special Report AR-307-E-E-2: Foreign Students in Japan, 1896-1947
subfiles.from: Education Research Branch, Research Unit, Analysis and Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Presents a historical study of foreign students in Japan, their national backgrounds, institutional support, and treatment from 1896 through 1947.
subfiles.summary: The introduction explains the report’s scope, limited sources, and reliance on interviews, questionnaires, and International Students Institute publications. It emphasizes Chinese students, students from Korea and Formosa, Southeast Asians recruited through the institute, and the wartime surveillance and discrimination experienced by foreign and colonial students. The first chapter links the arrival of large numbers of Chinese students to Japan’s victories over China and Russia, cultural and geographic proximity, and the demand for Western learning. It begins describing government admission regulations, the 1908 Sino-Japanese arrangements reserving places at selected institutions, and the poor living and educational conditions experienced by many privately funded Chinese students.
